# **CFTC and ETF Report** _A weekly update of futures and exchange traded fund activity._ • Gold was the most important of the precious metals at the start of September with platinum and silver following it step-for-step and only palladium asserting its independence. Gold proved to be a challenge for traders and analysts of nervous dispositions as the price sung about wildly both intraday and interday. Gold did recover enough ground to record a new high but has since weakened. Silver showed no independence and the gold:silver ratio changed little. Platinum performed very similarly to gold but lost a little ground relative to the yellow metal despite some potential impending supply side disruptions. Palladium was the quietest metal although even this traded in a wide range. Having failed to break the $800 barrier, it has since retreated closer to $720. • With prices somewhat more stable than in the previous week, despite the huge swings seen in trading throughout, net long speculative positions started to increase once more for all four metals. With the effects of the SGE and COMEX gold margin increases absorbed by the market, these changes are more reflective of underlying investor sentiment. • All of the precious metals recorded net inflows into their global Exchange Traded Funds in the week to the 9th of September. The amount of metal bought was unspectacular for all of the metals but this marked a gradual improvement in investor sentiment, something that was increasingly needed by palladium in particular. ##### **David Jollie** **david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **12 September 2011** ##### **New York:** 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 ##### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 ##### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 ##### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 ##### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | CFTC and ETF Weekly Report** **12 September 2011** ### **Gold CFTC data to 06 September 2011; ETF data to 9 September 2011.** #### **Exchange (COMEX and TOCOM) and ETF Gold Investment (oz)** ||**COMEX**

Although this was over $80 from its recent record levels, investors remained bullish and started to drive the price higher on the 2nd when US employment data underperformed expectations with, essentially, no new jobs created. Gold soared and held onto its gains in Asian trading with the US markets closed for Labor Day. Gold peaked at $1,920 on the 6th (another new record….) but news that the Swiss National Bank planned to link the Franc to the Euro drove a very rapid sell-off indeed that day, changing sentiment a little and sending gold back down to $1,810 on the 7th despite the improvement in its safe haven credentials. News that the German constitutional court had agreed that the Eurozone bailouts could legally go ahead removed the most immediate worries. However, leading up to the weekend, worries started to build over European sovereign debt once more. Rumours of an impending Greek default drove nervous gold buying and wide daily ranges, with gold pushing back to $1,880 before retreating below $1,840. - After the margin-driven liquidation of the previous week, net long speculative positions in gold started to build again. On COMEX, they increased by 1.13 million ounces to 28.6 million ounces with investors adding to their long positions in anticipation of further price rises. In Japan, TOCOM saw some selling and a gentle decline in net long exposure to 1.06 million ounces. - ETF investors continued quietly building their holdings of gold in the week to the 9th of September. They accumulated a further 84,000 ounces in taking the total amount of metal in ETF hands to 67.9 million ounces. #### **Gold Exchange Investment, April 09—September 11** 40 2,000 Gold price, $/oz

Silver reacted to the same macroeconomic stimuli as gold, acting as a second safe haven throughout. Trading was almost as difficult as for gold, with a range of $40.50 to $43.30. Silver started September at roughly $41.50 and leapt higher on the 2nd when US employment data hugely underperformed market expectations, coming to a halt above $43 late that day. Following the weekend, the Swiss foreign exchange intervention sent silver plummeting alongside gold to touch $40.65 on the 7th. It followed gold higher to $42.50 on the 9th but has since retreated, giving up all of these gains. - Silver saw keen buying by investors in the week to the 6th of September. Net long speculative positions on COMEX grew by 13.1 million ounces to a total of 281.1 million ounces. Both long and short positions held increased suggesting some mixed sentiment was present in the market. However, the bulls were the keener to get involved and long positions climbed by a little more than short positions. - Following light outflows of silver from ETF vaults in the previous week, investors started buying once again in the week to the 9th of September, driving their total metal holdings 2.7 million ounces higher to 454.8 million ounces. Most of the buying was in the iShares fund but most other funds saw small amounts of net buying. #### **Silver Exchange Investment, April 09—September 11** 450 50 Silver price, $/oz

- Once again, the near parity of platinum and gold in price terms was the main driving force behind price movements in the white metal. In fact, the ratio moved in gold’s favour a little as it performed its traditional “safe haven” role. There was no good economic news of note throughout the week and concerns over slowing growth and US unemployment buffeted platinum as did the Swiss decision to peg their currency to the Euro. Fundamentals such as ongoing wage negotiations and diverging opinions over Zimbabwean indigenisation had little price impact. Platinum climbed from $1,850 at the start of the month to $1,890 on the 5th and then a high of $1,895 on the 6th before

following gold obediently lower to $1,815 on the 7th. The prices were so tightly linked that platinum even followed when gold dropped like a metaphorical stone. Platinum rebounded to break $1,860 on the 8th and 9th before retreating back to its current $1,815. 2,500 2,000

- Net long speculative interest in platinum on NYMEX climbed by 124,000 ounces in the week to the 6th of September, taking positions to a record level of 1.76 million ounces. This rather overt bullishness seems to have been driven by the platinum:gold price ratio rather than by any fundamental story. TOCOM investors were happy to sell into this price strength, with net positions there shortening by 18,000 ounces to 431,000 ounces. - Platinum ETF holdings increased by 12,900 ounces in the week to the 9th of September, taking total metal holdings to a record 1.566 million ounces and more than reversing the previous week’s selling. Buying was split between North American and European investors. 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | CFTC and ETF Weekly Report** **12 September 2011** ### **Palladium CFTC data to 06 September 2011; ETF data to 9 September 2011.** ## **Exchange (Nymex and TOCOM) and ETF Palladium Investment (oz)** |**Date**|**Nymex**

Nonetheless, it has already traded in a range of $70 from a high to $790 to a low of $720. - Net long speculative positions in palladium on NYMEX rose by 50,000 ounces to 1.41 million ounces in the week to the 6th of September. After a decrease in investor interest at the start of August, they have now stabilised at close to 1.4 million ounces. This is, though, still half a million ounces longer than in late May, suggesting that a number of investors are happy to wait in expectation of later gains. - Net palladium Exchange Traded Fund flows were almost neutral in the week to the 9th of September. Holdings increased by 474 ounces to 2.13 million ounces. Although the weekly change in holdings is small, it marks some improvement of sentiment from the previous weeks’ selling. Nonetheless, the ETF Securities Fund saw net selling of 6,000 ounces.
